spec.purpose: Intake turns files in the record log into Records exactly once each, in id order, from every root the configuration names, and hands each to routing with a claim already held. It reads; it never writes a record.

section.title: What intake decides

node.title: Every record in every configured root is handed to routing exactly once across restarts, roots and the bash-to-Go cut-over, by a claim in a file ledger whose words the bash runner already writes

section.text: In: the directories of the record log. Out: a stream of (Record, claim) pairs in id order, one per record id, plus the ledger words that say what became of each.
Intake never reads a kind, a code or a note to decide anything: its only branches are on the file name, the ledger and the record's own seat.

section.title: Roots: where records are read
section.text: The bash runner watches one directory, the checkout's log, while seats in slots write into their own copy of the log, so a bus copies files across. Intake watches every root the configuration names and makes the copy unnecessary.
section.key: Directory patterns, variables resolved, globs allowed; the first pattern is the checkout's log. Each root holds year and month directories of record files.
section.text: A record id seen in two roots is one record: the root earliest in the list that holds it is Record.Root; a later copy of the same id is the same ledger entry and is never routed again.
A tick lists only the current and the previous month directory of each root, by UTC, and skips names that sort below the last id already seen in that root; a month turning needs no edit.
Every root is mounted read-only into the container; intake cannot write into a root even by mistake.
Polling, not inotify: file notification is not available on every filesystem WSL mounts, and a one second listing of a few thousand names costs nothing the line can feel.

section.title: The Source interface and the file source
section.text: Source is the interface: List(sinceID) returns new references across roots in id order; Read(ref) returns a Record or an unreadable error. The file source implements it now; a bus source later, and the ledger stays.
section.field: A reference is the id, the root it was first seen in and its path there; List never opens the file.
section.text: With the bus, List becomes a durable pull consumer's fetch and Read the message body; the claim in the ledger still decides exactly-once, so an at-least-once bus delivery is safe.
Ordering, dedupe across roots and the boundary filter are pure functions over lists of references; only the directory listing and the file read touch the file system.

section.title: Order and the first-start boundary
section.text: Ids sort by UTC second, then code, then a random suffix: two records in one second have no defined order, so nothing may depend on it; tests that depend on order write one second apart.
section.key: What the first start routes: now writes the start stamp as the boundary and routes only later records; start writes the zero stamp and routes the whole log. The boundary file in the state directory persists it.
section.text: A record whose id sorts below the boundary is never listed; a restart keeps the boundary file, so a log of old records never wakes every seat that ever existed.
In shadow mode the boundary is the shadow start, in the shadow state directory; going active adopts the bash runner's boundary and ledger, so the switch skips nothing and repeats nothing.

section.title: The routed ledger: claim before act
section.text: The ledger is one file per record id under the state directory's routed directory. Claim is an exclusive create of that file; the process that created it owns the record.
section.state: Written with the UTC at claim, before any job exists; a restart that finds it with no job files treats the record as interrupted.
The primary action reached done; the word is followed by the action name, exactly as the bash runner writes it.
The primary action was dead-lettered; a 500 note names it.
The first row said ignore; no job, no receipt, the ledger entry is the only trace.
No row matched; a 500 note to the monitor names the kind, the code and the id.
The record's seat is one of the scheduler's own seats; never routed, or a receipt would receipt itself without end.
The file did not parse or lacks a required field; a 500 note names it.
Claimed by a run that died before writing a job; a 500 note names it and the record is never repeated.
section.text: The words and the layout match the bash runner's ledger byte for byte, so the cut-over adopts the bash state directory and the parity report can compare the two ledgers.
The own test uses the configured list of runner seats, which holds the scheduler's seat and the bash runner's seat, so a receipt the bash runner wrote during shadow mode is never routed either.

section.title: Reading a record: what is checked, what is not
section.text: Read decodes the file into Record with unknown fields refused and the required fields present: schema version, id, at, code, seat, kind; the id must equal the file name and the patterns of id, at and code must hold.
Full schema validation is the lint's job on every file of the log, not the scheduler's at runtime; the scheduler checks the shape it reads and carries the rest through untouched.
A file that fails Read is ledgered unreadable with a 500 note naming the id; a file that appears and vanishes between List and Read is skipped and listed again next tick.
A record with no attempt field reads as attempt 1; absent optional fields read as empty strings or zero and are never written back.

section.title: Interrupted claims at start
section.text: At start, every ledger entry still claimed is examined: when job files exist for that record the jobs resume where they were; when none exist the entry becomes interrupted and one 500 note names it. Nothing is repeated silently.
The bash runner must abandon an interrupted record because its action was not durable; the scheduler's jobs are files, so a crash mid-action costs one retry, not the route.

section.title: The one writer: records go out through the executor

text.source: AGENTS.md#Hard rule: dated entry files, one file per entry; events/bin/event.sh

section.text: The scheduler writes no record file. Every record it emits (receipts, escalations, notes, policy defaults) is a record job whose verb runs the event writer on the host with the scheduler's seat and the flags the writer takes.
The executor forces the seat flag from its own configuration; the scheduler cannot write a record under another seat's name.
A record job that fails for good is a log line, never another record: a failed 500 note does not raise a 500 note, so a broken writer cannot flood the log.
Notes are cut to the writer's limit before the call; a note is for humans and nothing in the scheduler ever reads one back.

section.title: Keys this domain reads
section.key: Seconds between ticks; the belt is touched once per tick whatever the tick did.
Seats whose records are own: the scheduler's seat and the bash runner's seat.
The state directory; the ledger lives in its routed subdirectory and the boundary in its since file, as the bash runner lays them out.

section.title: Rows and codes this domain owns
section.owns-code: A record with 100 is accepted into the line: a seat is up or down, work started, a ticket was cut, a pull request opened. Intake accepts every record whatever its code; routing says what happens next.

section.title: Cases the build ticket proves

case.expected: exit 0: refs from two roots come back in id order, a duplicate id appears once with the first root

section.case: A record copied from a slot root into the checkout root is still one record.

case.expected: exit 0: a record below the boundary is never listed; since=start lists the whole log

section.case: A restart on an old log wakes nobody.

case.expected: exit 0: two concurrent Claim calls on one id return true once; the ledger file holds claimed and a UTC
exit 0: every word the bash runner writes is produced byte for byte by the Go ledger
exit 0: a file that does not parse is ledgered unreadable and yields one record job for a 500 note

section.case: A bad file is named once and never again.

case.expected: exit 0: a claimed entry with no job files becomes interrupted with one 500 note; one with job files is left for the job store

section.case: A crash between claim and job write is reported, not repeated.

case.expected: exit 0: a record whose seat is in runner_seats is ledgered own and never handed to routing

example.text: A tester in a slot writes test.passed into its slot's log; intake lists it from the slot root on the next tick and routing wakes the reviewer; the copy that the bus later puts in the checkout is the same id and is not routed.
The container is restarted while a seat bring-up job is running; at start the claimed entry has a job file, the job resumes with its next attempt, and no 500 is written.
Intake writes a receipt file itself because the executor socket was slow.
example.why: Two writers of one format; the lint cannot tell them apart.

example.text: A ledger that stores a cursor of the last routed id instead of one file per id.
example.why: Two records written in the same second sort by a random suffix; a cursor skips one.
